title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
authors: Mahish K. Guru, Mayank Nagar, Ayush vyas, Jan Bohlen, Roland Aydin, Noomane Ben Khalifa
abstract: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

infographic.key_insight: Co-PiLOT turns inverse design into constrained latent-space optimization by using a generative decoder as a feasibility prior and a physics-informed optimizer to search for target microstructures efficiently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a practical way to design magnesium alloy microstructures and textures under expensive crystal-plasticity simulation constraints, making it useful for computational materials and solid mechanics workflows.
method: ViT-based encoder compresses EBSD microstructure images into a low-dimensional latent space.
Generative decoders (latent diffusion / DiT / rectified flow) reconstruct high-fidelity candidate microstructures from latent codes.
MERIDIAN performs active optimization with deep-kernel GP uncertainty, feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an ~80,000-image EBSD dataset, ViT-FMDiT achieved the strongest reconstruction quality (FID 27.86, MS-SSIM 0.178) and, with MERIDIAN, reduced relative target error by 3–22% versus seven baselines within 160 simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on decoder fidelity and solver coupling, so any domain shift or weak reconstruction could constrain feasibility and transferability of the latent optimization results.
infographic.paper_title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design

title: Robustness of the Verwey transition against remanent strain-induced defects in magnetite
authors: M. A. Gala, K. J. Grzywa, K. Komędera, R. Zalecki, A. Baczmański, Z. Kąkol
abstract: The Verwey transition in magnetite is a benchmark electronically driven phase transition that is highly sensitive to lattice imperfections and external perturbations. Doping, deviations from oxygen stoichiometry, and irradiation-induced point defects are known to lower the Verwey transition temperature, $T_{\rm V}$. By contrast, the role of remanent strain fields and extended defect structures generated by uniaxial stress has remained largely unexplored. Here we combine dark-field x-ray microscopy (DFXM) and ac magnetic susceptibility to determine how strain-induced defects affect the Verwey transition in stoichiometric single-crystalline magnetite after uniaxial compression and unloading. The DFXM measurements were performed on two samples compressed along the same $[011]$ direction: loading to $200~\mathrm{MPa}$ generated stable line-like defects and remanent strain fields, whereas loading beyond the fracture threshold produced denser defect networks and mechanical fracture. To test the effect of a different loading geometry, we also measured the ac susceptibility of a sample fractured by compression along $[001]$. Real-space DFXM imaging, lattice-orientation mapping, and residual strain mapping show substantial remanent structural disorder after compression. Nevertheless, neither the transition temperature $T_{\rm V}$ nor the sharpness of the transition changes measurably in any of the compressed or fractured samples. This behavior contrasts with the strong suppression of $T_{\rm V}$ by point-like disorder. Our results show that extended line-like defects and remanent strain fields produced by plastic deformation do not measurably perturb the macroscopic electronic ordering responsible for the Verwey transition, thereby distinguishing the effects of point defects from those of extended slip-related defects in magnetite.

infographic.key_insight: Remanent strain fields and line-like slip defects created by compression do not measurably shift or broaden the Verwey transition in stoichiometric magnetite.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Extended plastic-deformation defects can be tolerated without degrading this key electronic phase transition, unlike point defects that strongly suppress it.
method: Compressed single-crystal magnetite along [011] and [001] to create remanent defects and fracture.
Used dark-field x-ray microscopy to map defects, lattice orientation, and residual strain after unloading.
Measured ac magnetic susceptibility to track the Verwey transition temperature and sharpness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across compressed and fractured samples, DFXM showed substantial residual disorder, but the measured Verwey transition temperature and transition sharpness were unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is specific to stoichiometric single-crystal magnetite and the tested loading geometries, so it may not generalize to other materials, defect types, or more severe damage states.
infographic.paper_title: Robustness of the Verwey transition against remanent strain-induced defects in magnetite

title: Fatigue failure in two-dimensional glasses under cyclic shear deformation
authors: Himangsu Bhaumik, Srikanth Sastry
abstract: We investigate fatigue failure in two-dimensional (2D) model glasses under cyclic shear deformation using atomistic simulations. We find that the number of cycles to failure diverges as a power law as the strain amplitude approaches the fatigue limit, with an exponent close to $-1$, in contrast to the exponent of $-2$ reported in three dimensions (3D). A failure exponent of $-1$ has also recently been observed in a 2D elastoplastic model, suggesting an interesting dependence on spatial dimensionality that needs to be rationalized. Measures of accumulated plastic activity, including dissipated work and non-affine displacements, exhibit scaling with the failure time that is consistent with results in 3D, and indicate a robust connection between damage accumulation and failure. To probe the origins of the variability of failure times, we perform isoconfigurational {\it seeded} simulations in which a localized soft region is introduced. While such seeding constrains the spatial location of failure, the distribution of failure times remains broad. These findings extend recent results in 3D concerning fatigue failure times to 2D glasses, including their relation to accumulated plasticity and apparent stochasticity, while also revealing a key difference, namely the exponent describing the divergence of the failure times.

infographic.key_insight: In 2D glasses under cyclic shear, the time to fatigue failure diverges as a power law near the fatigue limit with an exponent close to -1, indicating dimensionality changes how failure accelerates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests fatigue-life prediction in disordered solids may need dimension-aware models, while plastic-activity metrics still provide robust indicators of damage buildup before failure.
method: Atomistic simulations of 2D model glasses under cyclic shear deformation.
Measured failure cycles as strain amplitude approached the fatigue limit.
Used isoconfigurational seeded simulations with a localized soft region to probe variability and failure localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a power-law divergence of failure cycles near the fatigue limit, scaling of dissipated work and non-affine displacements with failure time, and a broad distribution of failure times even with seeding.
infographic.watch_item: Results are from 2D model glasses and may not transfer directly to real materials or to 3D systems without recalibration of the failure exponent and stochasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Fatigue failure in two-dimensional glasses under cyclic shear deformation

title: An Unfitted Hybrid High-Order Method for the Elastodynamics Problem with Imperfect Interface
authors: Peiqi Huang, Erik Burman
abstract: We design and analyse an unfitted hybrid high-order (HHO) method for the elastic wave equation in a medium made of two components separated by an imperfect interface of linear slip type, across which the traction is continuous and the displacement jump is proportional to the traction through a compliancy tensor $\bK=α\bI+(β-α)\bn\otimes\bn$. The mesh is not fitted to the interface: the discrete unknowns are doubled in the cut cells, the small cuts are cured by a cell agglomeration procedure, and no unknown is attached to the interface. The two specific ingredients of the method are a local symmetric strain reconstruction in each cut subcell, which incorporates the interface condition through the regularised interface stiffness $\bS_h=(h_Tδ^{-1}\bI+\bK)^{-1}$ in the spirit of Hansbo and Hansbo {\em{A finite element method for the simulation of strong and weak discontinuities in solid mechanics.}} {Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg.}, 193, 2004, and an interface stabilisation built from the same matrix. For the space semi-discrete problem we prove that the discrete bilinear form is coercive and continuous, and we derive an energy-error estimate of order $h^{k+1}$ and an $L^2$-error estimate of order $h^{k+2}$, with constants independent of the compliancy parameters and of how the interface cuts the mesh. The scheme is combined either with the Newmark scheme, which conserves a discrete energy exactly, or with singly diagonally implicit Runge--Kutta schemes of order up to four. Numerical experiments in two dimensions confirm the predicted convergence rates for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$, the robustness with respect to the compliancy over sixteen orders of magnitude, and illustrate the propagation of elastic waves across an unresolved slipping interface.

infographic.key_insight: An unfitted hybrid high-order method can accurately simulate elastodynamic wave propagation across an imperfect slipping interface without aligning the mesh to the interface.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method is robust for solid mechanics problems with unresolved internal interfaces, making it attractive for wave propagation and interface-dominated simulations in complex geometries.
method: Uses an unfitted HHO discretization with doubled unknowns in cut cells and cell agglomeration to handle small cuts.
Reconstructs symmetric strain locally in each cut subcell and enforces the imperfect interface through a regularized stiffness matrix.
Adds interface stabilization and couples the semi-discrete scheme with Newmark or high-order SDIRK time integration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal convergence in 2D tests, robustness over sixteen orders of magnitude in compliancy, and accurate wave transmission across the slipping interface for k=1,2,3.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and implementation may be sensitive to interface-cut geometry and the agglomeration/stabilization choices, especially in highly fragmented cut cells.
infographic.paper_title: An Unfitted Hybrid High-Order Method for the Elastodynamics Problem with Imperfect Interface

title: Fracture of Lattice Materials from Low to High Relative Density
authors: Adam P. Taylor, Sage Fulco, Kevin T. Turner
abstract: Lattice materials have highly tunable mechanical properties that are controlled by their internal geometry and base material behavior. While fracture models for low-density lattices are well-established, the fracture of lattices at relative densities above 30% remains largely unexplored. Here, we present an analytical model that combines homogenization methods and blunt-crack fracture theory to predict the fracture toughness of triangular and hexagonal lattices over a wide range of relative densities. Finite element modeling corroborates the analytical framework and demonstrates a shift in failure mechanisms between low and high relative density regimes. At high relative densities, failure is dominated by nodal stress concentrations, which are strongly influenced by the local crack-tip geometry and the macroscopic crack path. Significant stress redistribution is observed as the relative orientation and lattice fillet radius are varied, resulting in increased fracture toughness relative to baseline geometries. Furthermore, quasi-brittle poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) lattices achieve about a 1.6x enhancement in fracture toughness relative to perfectly brittle lattices as failure is delayed by localized plasticity. Notably, some quasi-brittle lattices are found to exceed the fracture toughness of their base material -- a feature only possible when the cell size is large compared to the base material's plastic radius. Experiments on lattice fracture specimens made from laser-cut PMMA validate the finite element results, but highlight the stochastic nature of failure in brittle lattice materials, especially at higher relative densities.

infographic.key_insight: Fracture toughness of triangular and hexagonal lattices is governed by a transition from density-dependent beam-level fracture at low relative density to nodal stress-concentration-driven failure at high relative density, enabling an analytical model across both regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designers can tune lattice toughness by adjusting relative density, crack orientation, and nodal fillet radius, with quasi-brittle base materials offering additional toughness gains through localized plasticity.
method: Homogenization-based analytical fracture model
Blunt-crack fracture theory for low-to-high relative density lattices
Finite element simulations plus PMMA fracture experiments
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite element results, analytical predictions, and laser-cut PMMA experiments jointly show good agreement and reveal a ~1.6× toughness increase for quasi-brittle lattices, with some cases exceeding base-material toughness.
infographic.watch_item: Brittle lattice fracture remains stochastic, especially at higher relative densities, so local geometry and crack-path variability must be considered in design and testing.
infographic.paper_title: Fracture of Lattice Materials from Low to High Relative Density

title: The Universal Classifier for Graph Learning
authors: Ben Finkelshtein, André Linhares, Petar Veličković, Bryan Perozzi, Mikhail Galkin
abstract: While foundation models have revolutionized natural language processing and computer vision by leveraging universal vocabularies, Graph Machine Learning (GML) remains fractured due to the absence of a unified feature and structural representation across diverse domains. Existing works claiming to be Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) are typically restricted to node-level predictions or require fixed feature dimensions, failing to provide a truly task-agnostic backbone for the full spectrum of graph learning applications. In this paper, we introduce the Universal Classifier (UC), which supports arbitrary feature and class cardinalities, unifying node-, edge-, and graph-level objectives under a single similarity-based classification objective. The UC reformulates all node-, edge-, and graph-level prediction tasks as maximizing similarity in the latent space: by lifting heterogeneous features and labels into 3D latent tensors, the model learns transferable features independent of specific input schemas. This architecture allows a single pre-trained model to generalize to node classification, node regression, and link prediction across unseen graphs with varying feature semantics. Experiments show strong zero-shot transfer performance across node-, link-, and graph-level tasks.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a Universal Classifier that turns node-, edge-, and graph-level graph learning into one similarity-based objective with arbitrary feature and class sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could simplify deployment of graph ML systems in engineering pipelines by providing a single transferable backbone across heterogeneous datasets and prediction tasks.
method: Lift heterogeneous node/edge/graph features and labels into 3D latent tensors.
Train with a shared latent similarity objective instead of task-specific heads.
Support zero-shot transfer across node classification, node regression, and link prediction on unseen graphs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong zero-shot transfer performance across node-, link-, and graph-level tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The main practical concern is whether the latent lifting and similarity formulation scales cleanly to large, highly sparse graphs and diverse feature schemas in real deployments.
infographic.paper_title: The Universal Classifier for Graph Learning

title: Cluster Attention Neural Operators for Solving Parametric Partial Differential Equations
authors: Ming Zhong, Antonio Colanera, Gianluigi Rozza, Zhenya Yan
abstract: Traditional simulations of parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) rely on repetitive computations for each parameter, which makes high-fidelity design impractical. Neural operators address this issue by learning solution operators, accelerating parameter-space mapping by orders of magnitude. Recent Transformer-based neural operators attempt to capture global dependencies, but often at the cost of quadratic attention complexity. Transolver resolves this problem by projecting physical states into a reduced slice space for attention computation. Although fast, this projection sacrifices fine spatial information. Moreover, by operating in this reduced space with shared weights across attention heads, it may constrain the model's flexibility, thereby limiting its capacity to capture complex phenomena. To address these issues, we propose the Cluster Attention Neural Operator (CANO), which reformulates attention via a novel cross-attention mechanism that dynamically clusters queries while preserving full-resolution keys and values. This avoids slice compression loss and removes weight-sharing limits. At the same time, the model remains fast without losing global interactions. Empirically, CANO achieves state-of-the-art performance across canonical PDE benchmarks, covering fluid and solid dynamics (e.g., Navier-Stokes, Airfoil, Plasticity), irregular unstructured geometries (e.g., Pipe Turbulence, Composites), and long-term temporal rollouts. Across solid deformation and turbulent flow benchmarks, CANO achieves lower errors than baselines and exhibits strong geometric adaptability and temporal consistency.

infographic.key_insight: CANO replaces costly global self-attention with clustered cross-attention to keep operator learning fast while preserving full-resolution spatial detail.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For parametric PDE simulation in solid mechanics and multiphysics, this offers a more accurate and scalable surrogate for design, analysis, and rapid what-if studies.
method: Dynamically clusters queries into compact attention groups
Uses full-resolution keys and values to avoid slice compression loss
Removes shared-weight constraints across attention heads for greater flexibility
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art results across multiple PDE benchmarks, including solid deformation and turbulent flow cases, with lower errors and strong temporal consistency.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on stable clustering quality and careful implementation on irregular meshes or long rollouts.
infographic.paper_title: Cluster Attention Neural Operators for Solving Parametric Partial Differential Equations

title: Stable and Interpretable Multi-Mode Rheological Universal Differential Equations (mmRUDEs) for Data-Driven Constitutive Modeling
authors: Mohua Das, Nicholas King, Navid Azizan, Gareth H. McKinley
abstract: The Rheological Universal Differential Equation (RUDE) framework embeds neural networks within a frame-indifferent tensorial constitutive backbone and so enables data-driven discovery of complex material rheological behavior. However, the flexibility that makes the RUDE framework attractive also makes it difficult to deploy: the learned neural network correction can make the constitutive equation numerically stiff during training, distribute corrections across non-unique combinations of tensor-basis terms, and extrapolate poorly with increasing nonlinearity, especially for industrially relevant materials with broad relaxation spectra. We develop a stability- and reliability-focused multi-mode RUDE framework that addresses three key challenges: thermodynamic admissibility, out-of-distribution prediction, and interpretability. Logarithmic compression of the input invariants and a split-network architecture improve numerical conditioning during training, while a differentiable projection layer enforces the Clausius--Duhem inequality at every time step. We illustrate the framework with both synthetic (a multi-mode Giesekus model) and experimental data on an entangled silicone polymer melt. Both models were trained on LAOS; they remain stable and accurate under unseen flow conditions, including steady shear, transient stress growth, and extensional flows, for which the unconstrained models may diverge numerically. To aid in interpretation of the contributions of each learned correction to the rheological behavior, we introduce the rheome, a compact way of representing the dominant weighted tensor-basis contributions to the overall rheological behavior. These improvements to the RUDE framework lead to stable and interpretable trained models, paving the way for implementation in computational fluid dynamics simulations and for guiding the rational design of soft material processing operations.

infographic.key_insight: mmRUDEs make neural constitutive laws more stable, thermodynamically admissible, and interpretable by combining a frame-indifferent tensor backbone with multi-mode corrections and constrained training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework improves reliable extrapolation for complex polymer and process flows, making data-driven rheology more usable in CFD and soft-material processing design.
method: Log-compress input invariants and use a split-network architecture to improve conditioning.
Apply a differentiable projection layer to enforce the Clausius--Duhem inequality at each time step.
Summarize learned tensor-basis contributions with the new “rheome” for interpretability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The models were trained on LAOS data for both a synthetic multi-mode Giesekus system and an entangled silicone polymer melt, and then tested successfully on unseen shear, stress-growth, and extensional flows.
infographic.watch_item: The added constraints and architecture still need careful implementation and validation to avoid over-constraining the model or limiting expressiveness on other material classes.
infographic.paper_title: Stable and Interpretable Multi-Mode Rheological Universal Differential Equations (mmRUDEs) for Data-Driven Constitutive Modeling

title: From Simulation to Fabrication: Realizing Silicon Crystalline Undulators with Silicon Nitride Stressor Layer Patterning
authors: L. Malagutti, L. Bandiera, F. Bonafè, N. Canale, D. De Salvador, P. Fedeli
abstract: A crystalline undulator is a crystal exhibiting periodic deformations that cause channeled particles to oscillate, generating coherent electromagnetic waves. In this study, stressor layer patterning has been employed to induce the desired deformations on a silicon substrate. Finite element method simulations were performed to optimize the geometric parameters of the undulator. The primary focus was on achieving sinusoidal deformation with sub-millimeter period and amplitude exceeding 1~nm, utilizing the silicon (110) plane for its superior channeling properties. Key parameters, such as substrate thickness and undulator period, were meticulously refined to ensure uniform deformation while minimizing the impact of higher harmonics, which could degrade performance. Based on the simulation results, a crystalline undulator, 160 $μ$m thick and consisting of 10 periods with a period length of 334 $μ$m, has been successfully fabricated. The final device demonstrates structural integrity and a uniform deformation extending up to 20 $μ$m from the surface. Specifically designed for use with 5-30 GeV particle beams, the undulator is capable of generating gamma photons in the 5-15 MeV range. This work effectively integrates advanced simulation techniques with precise fabrication methods, demonstrating the feasibility of crystalline undulators as high-performance devices for generating gamma radiation.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-element-guided stressor layer patterning can sculpt a silicon crystal into a near-sinusoidal crystalline undulator with sub-millimeter period and nanometer-scale amplitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This shows a practical path from simulation to fabrication for compact gamma-ray sources using standard silicon processing and controlled residual stress.
method: Simulated silicon substrate deformation with FEM to tune geometry and suppress higher harmonics.
Patterned a silicon nitride stressor layer to induce periodic bending on a silicon (110) substrate.
Fabricated a 160 µm-thick undulator with 10 periods and 334 µm period length based on the optimized design.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports successful fabrication and a uniform deformation extending up to 20 µm from the surface, with the device targeted to emit 5–15 MeV gamma photons under 5–30 GeV beams.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on maintaining highly uniform sinusoidal deformation; higher-order distortions or fabrication nonuniformity could reduce channeling quality and radiation output.
infographic.paper_title: From Simulation to Fabrication: Realizing Silicon Crystalline Undulators with Silicon Nitride Stressor Layer Patterning

title: Generalized Residual Closure: General Learning Dynamics for Stability-Plasticity Compatibility
authors: Dongxu Li, Yinuo Zhang, Hongyu Zhang, Feng Tian
abstract: Learning must acquire new capabilities while preserving both prior responsibilities and the capacity to learn again. We introduce Generalized Residual Closure (GRC), a framework for learning as recursive closure of future-relevant discrepancies: closing a residual establishes the conditions for subsequent prediction, interaction, and learning. Under a complete representation-relation description at a fixed learner-world boundary, persistent internal learning has two primitive modes: Transformation within a representation and revision of the Representation itself. We establish a local tangent decomposition under regularity assumptions and a criterion for when representation revision is necessary. In an affine model, we derive a necessary-and-sufficient condition for stability-plasticity compatibility and the unique solution of a constrained quadratic update problem, which preserves registered old responsibilities while reducing residuals with an effective safe response. We prove that reconstructive semantic protection weakly enlarges the safe-response operator relative to preserving an exact historical realization. Dynamic sufficiency and future-closure viability extend representation adequacy from current prediction to lawful future updating and continued learning. Growth Learning expands the lawful closure domain or lowers optimal closure cost without regression of the registered capability-cost frontier; a conditional commit rule maintains this order. Restricted-sector recoveries and a conditional representation theorem connect the framework to optimization, machine learning, and control. Together, these results organize adaptation, representation revision, and reusable capability within a common account of continued learning.

infographic.key_insight: GRC frames learning as recursively closing residual errors so an agent can both preserve prior responsibilities and remain able to learn new ones.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The paper offers a stability-plasticity criterion and update rule that are relevant for designing adaptive constitutive models and other systems that must revise representations without breaking prior behavior.
method: Defines a complete representation-relation view at a fixed learner-world boundary.
Separates internal learning into transformation within a representation versus revision of the representation.
Derives an affine constrained quadratic update with a unique safe-response solution and a criterion for when revision is required.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical derivations, local tangent decomposition, necessary-and-sufficient conditions, and proofs rather than experimental or dataset-based evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The framework relies on regularity and affine-model assumptions, so practical use may depend on whether a real system can satisfy or approximate those conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Generalized Residual Closure: General Learning Dynamics for Stability-Plasticity Compatibility

title: Two Routes to the Middle: Placement Search and Brain Readouts Converge on Where Continual Learners Should Specialize
authors: Yuan Huang, Zihan Chen, Runbin Zhang, Hongwei Ding, Changzeng Fu, Shiqi Zhao
abstract: Continual learners that keep a task-specific adapter in every block of a pre-trained vision transformer accumulate storage linearly with the number of tasks; keeping task-specific adapters in only a few blocks curbs this growth but raises the question of where to place them. We investigate this question from two perspectives. Algorithmically, training all contiguous four-block placements yields an inverted U: final accuracy peaks at intermediate depth and varies by up to 3.5 percentage points (pp), while inexpensive criteria based on weight spectra or activation statistics favor the deepest blocks. From neuroscience, the hierarchical organization and intermediate-stage plasticity of the visual cortex motivate us to ask whether a measurement taken outside the learner can guide layer specialization without placement search. LS-B observes the first tasks through a frozen fMRI encoding model of twelve human visual areas and commits task-specific capacity once to the blocks whose readouts vary most across tasks relative to their stable structure. Across three ViT-B/16 backbones, LS-B yields stable, backbone-specific allocations. On the two backbones with placement search, AugReg and iBOT, the selected blocks overlap the intermediate-depth region identified by search. Under matched storage and observation budgets, the selected blocks outperform the shallowest and deepest four-block configurations. On Split ImageNet-R, LS-B uses 60% of full-BiLoRA adapter storage while remaining within 1.5 pp of its final accuracy. The allocation requires no labels or backpropagation, adds under 0.6% runtime, and exhibits backbone-specific cortical signatures.

infographic.key_insight: Continual learners in vision transformers perform best when task-specific adapters are placed in intermediate blocks, and a frozen brain-readout signal can identify those blocks without expensive placement search.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to cut adapter storage and tuning cost in lifelong learning while preserving accuracy, especially when deploying compact task-specific modules in ViT backbones.
method: Search all contiguous four-block adapter placements and compare accuracy across depths.
Use LS-B: a frozen fMRI encoding model over 12 human visual areas to rank blocks by task-varying readouts versus stable structure.
Select one fixed placement per backbone and evaluate under matched storage and observation budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three ViT-B/16 backbones, the chosen blocks align with intermediate-depth regions, and on Split ImageNet-R LS-B uses 60% of full-BiLoRA storage while staying within 1.5 pp of final accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The allocation is backbone-specific and derived from fMRI-based readouts, so transferring the same placement rule to a new architecture or domain may require recalibration.
infographic.paper_title: Two Routes to the Middle: Placement Search and Brain Readouts Converge on Where Continual Learners Should Specialize

title: PoliVEM: a Python-driven virtual element framework for computational solid mechanics
authors: Paulo Akira F. Enabe, Rodrigo Provasi
abstract: This work presents PoliVEM, a software framework for the Virtual Element Method (VEM) in computational solid and structural mechanics. A C++17 computational core and a Python interface place one-dimensional beams, two- and three-dimensional elasticity, axisymmetric elasticity, transient diffusion, and finite-strain hyperelasticity in a common implementation. The framework stores vertex, edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom in one hierarchy, constructs the energy, strain, and $L^2$ projections from common polynomial data, and retains the consistency--stabilization split at the element level. The core separates the mesh, material, element, assembler, and solver responsibilities and combines them by composition. A new formulation supplies its projection, discrete form, and stabilization while reusing the mesh representation, degree-of-freedom numbering, boundary-condition treatment, sparse assembly, algebraic solvers, and Python binding pattern. The numerical infrastructure includes polygonal and polyhedral mesh input, higher-order entity numbering, cached projection operators, static condensation, coloured sparse assembly, linear solver selection based on the matrix structure, an incremental Newton method with line search and regularization, and explicit and implicit time integration. Three numerical experiments examine the shared implementation through polynomial reproduction, recovery after static condensation, higher-order degree-of-freedom handling, polygonal and polyhedral meshes, patch tests, stiffness spectra, and comparisons with independent finite element calculations. The results verify the common core for the beam and two- and three-dimensional elasticity formulations. They also identify the scaling of high-order polynomial bases on anisotropic cells and the memory required by sparse direct factorizations as the main limitations of the current implementation.

infographic.key_insight: PoliVEM unifies multiple solid-mechanics virtual element formulations in a single Python-driven C++ framework by reusing common mesh, DOF, projection, assembly, and solver infrastructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical, extensible foundation for polygonal and polyhedral analysis of beams, elasticity, diffusion, and hyperelasticity with consistent element-level treatment.
method: Common C++17 core with Python interface for modular VEM solvers
Shared hierarchy for vertex/edge/face/cell DOFs plus cached projection operators
Supports static condensation, coloured sparse assembly, Newton solving, and time integration
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper validates the framework with polynomial reproduction, recovery after static condensation, higher-order DOF handling, patch tests, stiffness spectra, and comparisons to independent finite element results.
infographic.watch_item: High-order polynomial bases can scale poorly on anisotropic cells, and sparse direct factorization memory can become a limiting cost.
infographic.paper_title: PoliVEM: a Python-driven virtual element framework for computational solid mechanics

title: Aligning feature-mapping designs to given density fields, first and second order
authors: Fabian Wein, Patrick Jung, Arash Moradian, Michael Stingl
abstract: Feature-mapping methods represent structural designs by explicit geometric primitives on fixed analysis grids, an interpretable and parametric alternative to the density fields of density-based topology optimization (SIMP). In contrast to SIMP, however, feature-mapping optimization is sensitive to the initial design. We present a gradient-based approach to align a feature-mapping configuration to a given (pseudo) density field, e.g., to initialize a subsequent feature-mapping optimization. The staged approach is based on a least-squares tracking formulation, preceded by a variant that only rewards alignment and does not penalize mismatch. Without an underlying finite element simulation, iterations are cheap, but isolated features receive little sensitivity information. As a remedy, we propose an asymmetric transition function based on automatically parametrized Bézier curves. We demonstrate the approach for a 2D cantilever and the five-bar design; for the latter, we show optional feature minimization based on the feature scaling variable of the geometry projection method. The approach works well with first-order optimizers. The absence of a state problem and the small number of variables, however, also make a second-order formulation attractive. To the best of the authors' knowledge, we present the first Hessian formulation for feature mapping and report the behavior of first- and second-order optimizers on our benchmark problems. For completeness, we also give the exact Hessian of the state-based compliance, which requires one additional solution of the FEM system per feature variable.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a gradient-based alignment method that fits a feature-mapping design to a target density field before optimization, improving initialization for interpretable geometry-based structural design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical bridge between density-based topology optimization and parametric feature mapping, making structural design more robust, faster to initialize, and potentially better suited for engineering workflows.
method: Use a staged alignment scheme: first maximize overlap, then switch to least-squares tracking against the target density field.
Introduce an asymmetric transition function based on automatically parametrized Bézier curves to better handle isolated features.

Derive first- and second-order formulations, including the first Hessian for feature mapping, and test first- vs second-order optimizers; optional feature minimization is supported via the geometry projection method.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is demonstrated on two benchmark problems—a 2D cantilever and a five-bar design—with reported behavior of first- and second-order optimizers, including exact compliance Hessians for completeness.
infographic.watch_item: Because the approach has no underlying state problem, isolated features can receive weak sensitivity information, so the transition design and optimizer choice matter for convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Aligning feature-mapping designs to given density fields, first and second order

title: Neural topology optimization of ship structures under propulsion machinery vibrations
authors: Shengyu Yan, Muhammad Muztahidul Hakim Zareer, Jasmin Jelovica
abstract: Ship structural vibrations contribute to noise, fatigue, and equipment damage, while dynamic-compliance topology optimization can produce pathological designs near resonance. This study extends neural-reparameterized topology optimization using a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KATO) to forced-vibration design with active input power (AIP) as the objective. Applications include a 100 Hz engine-supporting deck panel and an 18 Hz thruster foundation frame. Helmholtz PDE filtering and Heaviside projection control feature sizes and manufacturing tolerance. Across both deck families, all eight optimized layouts reduce AIP relative to size-optimized references and, after finite-depth extrusion, also achieve lower static compliance. For unrestricted, manufacturing-aware, and stress-aware frame variants, KATO matches GCMMA in AIP within 0.5 dB while yielding 22-36x lower static compliance after matched-volume binary re-analysis. In a near-resonant 300 Hz case, both methods reduce initial AIP by more than 32 dB; KATO maintains a connected design, achieves 59x lower binary static compliance, and reduces maximum AIP over 1-500 Hz by 2.7 dB. KATO runs 6.4-10.4x faster than GCMMA for the implemented stress-aware formulations. The results demonstrate neural AIP-driven topology optimization as an efficient approach for designing connected, feature-size-controlled ship structures with improved forced-vibration performance.

infographic.key_insight: A neural topology optimization method using KATO can design ship structures with lower forced-vibration active input power while keeping layouts connected and manufacturable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables lighter, feature-controlled ship panels and foundations that better resist propulsion-induced vibrations, noise, fatigue, and equipment damage.
method: Uses a convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KATO) to parameterize topology optimization.
Optimizes active input power (AIP) under forced vibration, with Helmholtz filtering and Heaviside projection for feature-size control.
Benchmarks against GCMMA and evaluates multiple ship-structure cases, including near-resonant behavior and stress-aware designs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across deck and frame cases, KATO reduced AIP relative to size-optimized references, matched GCMMA within 0.5 dB in frame variants, and in a near-resonant case cut peak AIP by more than 32 dB while improving static compliance and runtime.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on careful filtering, projection, and matched-volume re-analysis; near-resonant optimization can still be sensitive to formulation and manufacturing constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Neural topology optimization of ship structures under propulsion machinery vibrations

title: Averaging in thermodynamic dislocation theory: general macroscopically uniform stress and strain states
authors: Khanh Chau Le
abstract: The averaging procedure, developed for polycrystalline bars under axially symmetric tension or compression, is extended to arbitrary macroscopically uniform stress and strain states. Starting from the equal probability hypothesis for grain orientations, the mean resolved shear stress and the mean resolved elastic and plastic shear strains are defined as root-mean-square averages over all slip-system orientations. Two exact identities for isotropic orientation averages show that the mean resolved shear stress is proportional to the von Mises equivalent stress, and that the direction of macroscopic plastic flow, obtained from the hypothesis that the plastic slip rate on a system is proportional to the resolved shear stress acting on it, is the stress deviator. The result is an associated $J_2$ flow theory whose hardening law is not fitted but follows from the kinetics of thermally activated dislocation depinning and the evolution equations for the dislocation density and the effective disorder temperature of thermodynamic dislocation theory, written as rates with respect to time so that arbitrary loading paths can be followed. For torsion the theory yields the torque--twist relation of bars and tubes without the classical reductions to a shear stress--strain curve. The parameters for copper are identified jointly from Hopkinson-bar tension, dynamic compression at room and elevated temperatures, and torque--twist records at several twist rates. One set of material parameters, consistent with the earlier compression-only identification, describes tension, compression and torsion from room temperature to $1173$\,K and from $10$ to $2300$\,s$^{-1}$ to $6$\,\% rms over 142 data points; the tension--torsion discrepancy noted by Johnson and Cook is traced to the initial dislocation state of their torsion specimens.

infographic.key_insight: The paper generalizes thermodynamic dislocation theory to arbitrary uniform stress and strain states, showing that macroscopic plastic flow emerges as an associated J2 theory with hardening governed by dislocation kinetics rather than empirical fitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a single physics-based constitutive framework that can predict tension, compression, and torsion of copper across wide temperature and strain-rate ranges using one parameter set.
method: Extend orientation averaging from axial loading to general macroscopic stress/strain states using equal-probability grain orientations.
Use root-mean-square averages of resolved shear stress and shear strains over slip-system orientations.
Couple the averaged flow rule to thermally activated dislocation depinning, dislocation density evolution, and effective disorder temperature evolution in time rate form.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was calibrated on Hopkinson-bar tension, dynamic compression, and torque-twist data, and one parameter set matched 142 data points within about 6% rms over 10 to 2300 s^-1 and room temperature to 1173 K.
infographic.watch_item: The framework depends on the assumed initial dislocation state and equal-orientation averaging, so specimen history and texture effects may need careful treatment in new materials or loading paths.
infographic.paper_title: Averaging in thermodynamic dislocation theory: general macroscopically uniform stress and strain states

title: Running error bounds in finite element kernels
authors: Michal Habera, Paul T. Kühner, Matteo Croci, Andreas Zilian
abstract: Rounding errors in finite element computations can lead to a complete loss of accuracy, stalled convergence, and incorrect results. Moreover, the effects of rounding errors accumulated within automatically generated and compiled kernels are difficult to analyze a priori. We present the first software framework for automated rounding error estimation within finite element kernels. The proposed methodology is based on an a posteriori technique called Running Error Analysis (REA), where a forward error estimate is automatically computed concurrently with the value. An open-source implementation is provided for the FEniCS Form Compiler (FFCx), based on a C++ backend for generating type-generic templated kernels over a custom arithmetic type that tracks both the value and its error estimate. We demonstrate REA on two examples. First, we use it to detect catastrophic cancellation in the assembly of a Neo-Hooke hyperelastic model in the small deformation regime. A series expansion circumvents the cancellation problem and the computed error estimates show this. Second, we study the assembly of the Laplace operator on a near-degenerate mesh. We demonstrate that our REA implementation typically incurs only 2-4x performance overhead. Applications of this work include robust reduced-precision computations in embedded systems, numerical debugging of new, possibly ill-conditioned or unstable PDE formulations, and guiding the design of mixed-precision kernels.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces an automated way to estimate floating-point rounding error inside finite element kernels while the kernel computes its value, helping catch accuracy loss before it breaks a simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes FEM code more reliable for nonlinear mechanics, ill-conditioned meshes, reduced-precision workflows, and kernel debugging in production solvers.
method: Wrap kernel arithmetic in a custom type that carries both value and running forward-error estimate.
Integrate the approach into the FEniCS Form Compiler (FFCx) via a C++ backend that generates type-generic templated kernels.
Use Running Error Analysis (REA) to compute an a posteriori error bound concurrently with each finite element operation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors validate the framework on a Neo-Hooke hyperelasticity cancellation case and a near-degenerate Laplace assembly, reporting typical runtime overhead of only about 2–4x.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds overhead and depends on kernel-generation integration, so it may need careful tuning for large-scale or performance-critical HPC workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Running error bounds in finite element kernels

title: Explainable Machine Learning for Multilayer Planar Winding Inductance Estimation
authors: Spyros Rigas, Theofilos Papadopoulos, Georgios Alexandridis, Antonios Antonopoulos
abstract: Rapid and accurate self-inductance estimation for multilayer rectangle-shaped planar windings is essential for modern high-frequency power converters, yet traditional workflows rely on complex mathematical equations, rigid monomial formulas or unexplainable black-box machine learning (ML) models that degrade severely outside their training domain. This paper introduces an explainable ML framework unifying post-hoc feature attribution (SHAP and permutation importance) with Kolmogorov-Arnold Network-guided symbolic regression via the SR-KAN framework to discover closed-form analytical equations without prior structural assumptions. Evaluated on a new open-source dataset of over 10,000 Finite Element Analysis (FEA) simulations across seven out-of-distribution (OOD) classes, standard tree-based ensembles exhibit severe extrapolation errors (> 36%), whereas the unconstrained SR-KAN expression achieves a robust OOD relative error of 8.22%. Experimental verification across 55 physical printed circuit board prototypes (up to 8 layers, with inductances from 4.11 μH to 559.27 μH) confirms that the KAN-discovered expression translates effectively to real-world hardware, predicting inductance with a mean absolute relative error of 6.26%. To support reproducible research, the complete FEA simulation dataset and prototype measurements are released open-source.

infographic.key_insight: An explainable ML workflow combining SHAP, permutation importance, and SR-KAN symbolic regression can recover a closed-form inductance formula that generalizes far better than standard black-box models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, accurate self-inductance estimation for multilayer planar windings, reducing reliance on costly FEA or rigid hand-derived equations in high-frequency power converter design.
method: Built an open-source FEA dataset with 10,000+ simulations spanning seven OOD test classes.
Used feature attribution methods to interpret which geometric variables matter most.
Applied KAN-guided symbolic regression to discover an analytical inductance expression without preset formula structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 55 PCB prototypes and 10,000+ FEA cases, the SR-KAN expression achieved 8.22% OOD relative error on simulations and 6.26% mean absolute relative error on hardware, while tree ensembles exceeded 36% OOD error.
infographic.watch_item: The learned formula is still data-dependent, so accuracy may drop for winding geometries or operating conditions outside the released dataset and validated prototype range.
infographic.paper_title: Explainable Machine Learning for Multilayer Planar Winding Inductance Estimation

title: FracGen: Learning How Objects Stretch and Tear with Physics-Informed Video Generation
authors: Trong-Tung Nguyen, Jiahan Zhang, Anand Bhattad
abstract: We introduce FracGen, a fracture-aware video generation model that produces plausible, controllable fracture dynamics from a single image of an intact object, conditioned on physics signals. To train FracGen, we build FracSim, a fracture-aware simulation framework that augments material point method (MPM) simulation with a continuum damage model, producing paired fracture videos and dense, pixel-aligned physical fields at no additional cost beyond standard rendering. FracGen leverages these maps in two ways: it is trained to jointly predict them alongside RGB video, encouraging the model to capture physical state rather than surface appearance; and it is supervised with physics-informed losses that encourage consistency among the predicted maps. As a result, FracGen captures distinct material-specific fracture behavior without expensive test-time simulation or per-scene tuning, while offering fine-grained control over where an object tears, how fast the crack propagates, and how much deformation precedes failure. We further introduce a benchmark for evaluating the physical plausibility of generated fracture video, and show through extensive experiments that FracGen outperforms existing video generation baselines in both physical and visual fidelity. Results are best viewed in our project website: https://fracgen.github.io/.

infographic.key_insight: FracGen learns fracture dynamics from a single intact image by conditioning video generation on physics signals, enabling controllable tearing and deformation without per-scene simulation at test time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a practical way to synthesize physically plausible fracture videos for design, testing, and analysis of brittle or deformable materials with less reliance on expensive experimental capture or simulation.
method: Builds FracSim, an MPM-based fracture simulation pipeline with a continuum damage model to generate paired fracture videos and dense physical fields.
Trains FracGen to jointly predict RGB video and physics maps, so the model learns physical state rather than only appearance.
Uses physics-informed losses to enforce consistency among predicted fracture, deformation, and damage fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports a new benchmark for physical plausibility and states that FracGen outperforms prior video generation baselines in both visual fidelity and physical fidelity.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and realism of the simulated supervision, so domain gaps between FracSim and real materials may limit generalization.
infographic.paper_title: FracGen: Learning How Objects Stretch and Tear with Physics-Informed Video Generation

title: Behavioral Convergence Without Representational Convergence: Persistent Training-History Dependence in Neural Networks
authors: Ertuğrul Mutlu
abstract: Neural networks trained toward the same final objective can reach similar predictive performance while retaining internal representations shaped by earlier training history. We study this effect using controlled sequential-training experiments in which paired convolutional networks start from identical weights, experience reversed task orders, and then receive the same deterministic common-relaxation distribution. Across 20 paired MNIST runs, 16 satisfy a predeclared behavioral-matching criterion, yet their matched representations retain a mean history score of 0.139 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.127-0.153) and approximately 3.1% prediction disagreement. Extending common relaxation to 50,000 optimizer updates does not erase the measured difference: across five paired seeds, the representation-history score remains 0.190 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.161-0.219) at the end of the measured horizon while the mean accuracy gap is only 0.18 percentage points. Fresh linear probes show that, with sufficient labeled data, the two histories retain practically equivalent linearly accessible class information. A same-label rotated-MNIST control reproduces the effect: all five paired seeds reach behavioral matching while retaining a mean representation-history score of 0.162. Finally, a matched-learning-rate ReLU-LeakyReLU control reduces the 50,000-update representation residue by 0.040 on average in all five paired seeds, providing directional evidence that activation-mediated plasticity contributes to the persistence of training-history effects. These results provide protocol-scoped evidence that behavioral convergence need not imply representational convergence and that optimization history can leave measurable internal traces after prolonged common training.

infographic.key_insight: Neural networks can become behaviorally similar on the same task while still carrying distinct internal representations shaped by their earlier training history.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI-enabled engineering workflows, matching accuracy alone may hide persistent path dependence, so internal-state checks are important when comparing trained models.
method: Paired CNNs start from identical weights and train on tasks in reversed order.
Both models then undergo the same deterministic common-relaxation training distribution.
Controls test longer relaxation, rotated MNIST, and ReLU vs. LeakyReLU effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 20 paired MNIST runs, 16 met the behavioral-matching criterion, yet the mean representation-history score remained 0.139 with about 3.1% prediction disagreement; similar persistence held in longer-relaxation and control experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The results are protocol-scoped, so the persistence of history effects may depend on the architecture, training schedule, and data regime used.
infographic.paper_title: Behavioral Convergence Without Representational Convergence: Persistent Training-History Dependence in Neural Networks

title: Continual Reinforcement Learning with Neuroevolution
authors: Eleni Nisioti, Andrea Cossu, Kathrin Korte, Sebastian Risi
abstract: Despite many studies about causes and remedies of plasticity loss in Reinforcement Learning (RL) under continual task changes, no RL method has yet consistently achieved a good balance between adaptation and forgetting. Here we turn to an alternative optimization paradigm, neuroevolution (NE): algorithms that search directly in weight space through mutation and selection over a population of neural networks. Across a wide array of environments and environmental changes, with policies ranging from a few hundred parameters to million-parameter networks, we compare evolution strategies (ES) and genetic algorithms (GAs) against state-of-the-art continual RL variants and population-based RL. ES most consistently achieves a good stability-plasticity trade-off, while the GA is the most plastic method but forgets more than ES. To explain this, we study the return landscape around each method's solutions. ES finds the widest neighborhoods, i.e.\ regions of weight space in which perturbed policies still solve the task, and the size of the overlap between the neighborhoods of consecutive tasks correlates with a method's stability-plasticity trade-off. Rewarding behavioral diversity in a GA through novelty search makes the population even more plastic, at the cost of forgetting. Finally, symptoms of plasticity loss commonly reported in RL do not transfer to NE. Overall, these results establish NE as a competitive alternative to RL under continual task changes, and suggest that training under perturbations in weight space may be a useful mechanism for continual learning more broadly.

infographic.key_insight: Neuroevolution, especially evolution strategies, offers a stronger stability-plasticity balance than standard continual RL methods by optimizing directly in weight space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For adaptive control and sequential decision systems, this suggests a practical route to continual learning that can retain prior capabilities while adapting to new operating conditions.
method: Compare evolution strategies and genetic algorithms against continual RL and population-based RL across multiple changing environments.
Analyze return landscapes around learned policies to measure how wide and overlapping task-solution neighborhoods are in weight space.
Test whether novelty search increases plasticity and examine how perturbation robustness relates to forgetting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study evaluates a wide range of environments and task changes, from a few hundred to million-parameter policies, and links overlap of solution neighborhoods to stability-plasticity performance.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest plasticity gains can come with increased forgetting, so deployment should consider how much prior-task retention is acceptable.
infographic.paper_title: Continual Reinforcement Learning with Neuroevolution
